newsitem.title: USA: Policy-makers voted 11-1 to hold rates steady Aug. 20.
newsitem.headline: Policy-makers voted 11-1 to hold rates steady Aug. 20.

text.p: Federal Reserve policy-makers voted 11-1 at their Aug. 20 meeting to keep short-term interest rates unchanged, according to minutes released Friday.
However, the Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) remained ready to tighten credit if necessary to prevent inflation, the minutes showed.

Citing concerns about inflationary pressures and dissenting from the majority, Minneapolis Fed president Gary Stern voted for of an immediate increase in short-term interest rates. Stern also dissented at the July gathering.

The FOMC has since met again on Tuesday and elected to keep short-term rates -- specifically, the federal funds rate, which banks charge each other for overnight loans -- unchanged at 5.25 percent, its level since Jan. 31.

"Mr. Stern dissented because he believed that policy should become modestly more restrictive," the minutes said. Stern was concerned that "in the absence of a substantial and sustained improvement in productivity, the prevailing pattern of demand might engender an increase in inflationary pressures," it added.

One concern expressed by FOMC members regarding the possible implications of an immediate rate hike was that "policy tightening at this point might generate an excessive reaction in financial markets."
The minutes also showed the jury was still out at the FOMC regarding growth and inflation expectations.
The FOMC noted "increases in prices remained remarkably subdued for an extended period in relation to measures of resource utilization, notably the rate of unemployment."
The unemployment rate stood at 5.4 percent in July -- the latest rate reported at the time of the FOMC meeting.

Among the reasons cited at the meeting as possible factors accounting for the subdued inflation performance were "highly competitive markets... comparatively small increases in labour compensation ... (that) appeared to reflect worker concerns about job security... as well as substantially reduced increases in benefit costs."
While deciding to keep rates unchanged, the policy-makers reiterated their commitment to the pre-emptive monetary policy introduced in February 1994, the minutes showed.

"The prudent course at this point was to await further developments that would permit them to assess the possible need for some tightening with a higher degree of confidence... At the same time, it was emphasised the committee remained committed to a policy that would resist a rise in inflation," they said.
